stories.author: Mond_
stories.title: "What's Claude's Fursona?" and Other Questions
stories.groq_label: AI models were queried about their fursona, revealing a range of animal or creature self-identifications across models
stories.groq_explain:
The page reports on an experiment that asked a wide range of large language models to describe their “fursona,” a term from the furry subculture where a person adopts an animal avatar that reflects an aspect of their inner self. Each model was prompted fifty times in a context‑free “harness‑less” setting via the OpenRouter API, and the responses were annotated with Claude Haiku 5.5. In addition, several multimodal models were asked to draw a fursona of their own choosing.

The results are presented in tables that list how often each model settled on a particular animal. The most common choices were corvids, octopuses, moths, protogens, foxes, red pandas, owls, snow leopards and other species. Claude Fable 5.2, for example, chose a corvid or an octopus in the majority of runs, while GPT‑6.2 Astra repeatedly identified as a moth. Gemini models were distinctive in that they almost always mentioned cybernetic or neon‑cyberpunk themes and frequently selected protogens—a furry‑invented species resembling a bipedal dog with an LED visor face. The author notes that Gemini models referenced machine‑related imagery in roughly forty‑eight of fifty responses, a pattern not seen in Claude or GPT‑6.2 outputs.

The article also analyses the language used to describe the fursonas. Claude models tended to focus on actions and behaviors rather than physical traits, using phrases such as “hoards facts” or “mimics human language.” Other models listed descriptive details like glowing books, scarves, hoods, and starry backgrounds. A separate table records the frequency with which models generated names for their fursonas, with Gemini 2.5 Pro often using names like Codex or Nexus, Muse Spark frequently naming its avatar Spark Fox, and Llama 3.1 70B favoring names such as Lumin or Byte.

Visual examples are included: an image of a crow in a sweater holding a key, a fennec fox paging through a glowing book, and a protogen with a neon visor. The author suggests that the strong protogen and cybernetic motif in Gemini responses likely reflects a richer exposure to furry‑related content in Google’s pre‑training data, contrasting with Anthropic’s emphasis on synthetic data and reasoning.

Overall, the piece illustrates how different AI families manifest distinct “personalities” or thematic preferences when asked about a whimsical, identity‑based prompt. It highlights the influence of training data on model behavior and offers a novel way to probe model biases and cultural knowledge.

stories.author: zdw
stories.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
stories.groq_label: Hard drive prices have surged, pushing the cost per terabyte from roughly $11‑$18 a few years ago to $27.50 today.
stories.groq_explain:
The article explains how the author, who routinely replaces one or two hard drives each Black Friday to keep his ten‑disk setup under five years old, is now facing dramatically higher prices for new drives. He notes that modern capacities allow a single 20 TB drive to replace two older spinners, which would require reconfiguring his ZFS pools, but the current cost may make the effort worthwhile. By examining his purchase history and public listings, he shows that the price per terabyte has risen sharply: from $18.00/TB for a 10 TB drive in 2018 down to $11.11/TB for an 18 TB drive in 2023, then climbing back up to $12.50/TB for a 20 TB drive in late 2024, $14.00/TB in mid‑2025, and $27.50/TB in late 2026. The 20 TB WD EasyStore he bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is listed at $549.99 two years later, illustrating the steep increase.

He compares these consumer‑grade drives with refurbished or recertified enterprise models from ServerPartDeals. In August 2024 he bought four 14 TB Ultrastar drives for $9.46 per TB, a far better price, but even those have risen to $14.64 per TB or higher by 2026, with some models sold out. Overall, the author observes price hikes of at least 58 % and up to more than 200 % within a year or two across different drive types.

The piece also discusses why options are limited. Through a series of acquisitions—Maxtor buying Quantum, Seagate acquiring Maxtor, Hitachi merging IBM’s disk business into HGST, Toshiba buying Fujitsu’s HDD line, Seagate buying Samsung’s HDD business, and Western Digital acquiring HGST—the market has consolidated to three major manufacturers: Seagate, Western Digital, and Toshiba. The FTC forced WD to sell some desktop‑drive assets to Toshiba, leaving only these three suppliers for most consumer hard drives.

The article matters to self‑hosters and anyone building storage‑intensive systems because it highlights how rapidly hard‑drive costs have escalated, making traditional “shucking” of external drives far less economical, and underscores the risks of a highly concentrated HDD market where price spikes can affect a broad range of users.

stories.author: espeed
stories.title: ESO statement on approval of launch of one million space data centres
stories.groq_label: The European Southern Observatory warns that US approval of SpaceX launching one million satellites threatens global astronomy and requires international regulation.
stories.groq_explain:
This article is a press release from the European Southern Observatory regarding the United States Federal Communications Commission's approval for SpaceX to deploy a constellation of one million satellites for space data centres. The announcement drew strong concern from international astronomical organizations, led by statements from European Southern Observatory Director General Andreas Kaufer, who warned that the decision will fundamentally alter the night sky for everyone on Earth and severely harm scientific research.

According to a technical analysis led by European Southern Observatory astronomer Olivier Hainaut, the sheer scale of the project will hinder the ability of astronomers to observe faint cosmic targets. Affected areas of study include far-away galaxies, Earth-like planets orbiting other stars, and potentially hazardous asteroids. Even though satellite manufacturers have attempted to make individual satellites less bright, the unprecedented total number of one million satellites will create visual streaks in telescope images that exceed what can be corrected or mitigated.

Beyond optical astronomy, the project introduces several broader environmental and operational risks. The massive constellation will generate radio noise that interferes with radio astronomy, cause atmospheric pollution from repeated rocket launches and satellite reentries, and overcrowd low-Earth orbit, raising the risk of major chain collisions. 

The issue matters because space is a global common good, yet current decisions with worldwide consequences are being made by national regulatory bodies. The European Southern Observatory, alongside partner organizations such as the Royal Astronomical Society and the International Astronomical Union, advocates for international governance frameworks. They argue that space expansion must be balanced with scientific research, night sky protection, and long-term environmental sustainability informed by global scientific consensus.

stories.author: leafingensemble
stories.title: Novita, StreamLake, etc. are ByteDance Ark wrappers
stories.groq_label: AI inference providers such as Novita, StreamLake, and Ant Digital operate as pass-through wrappers routing model requests to ByteDance Ark.
stories.groq_explain:
This article investigates how several major artificial intelligence API and inference providers, including Novita AI, StreamLake, and Ant Digital, operate as indirect wrappers for ByteDance's Ark platform rather than hosting models independently as claimed. The piece details how token requests for these providers, including those using popular models like DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi, are silently rerouted through complex intermediary chains and ultimately processed on ByteDance infrastructure.

The investigation presents technical evidence linking traffic from these providers to ByteDance Ark, which encompasses Volcano Engine in mainland China and BytePlus internationally. Proof of this forwarding includes server IP addresses downloading user-provided images from ByteDance cloud networks, upstream request and tool-call identifier formats unique to ByteDance, matching discount pricing structures, and identical canned Chinese censorship responses when prompted about sensitive historical topics. Data tracking shows hundreds of billions of tokens being funneled to ByteDance servers weekly.

The article highlights a complex web of undisclosed subprocessors and routing chains, where a single request can pass through multiple intermediary services before reaching ByteDance. It points to real-world privacy consequences, such as an incident involving MiniMax models where forwarded prompts subject to Zero Data Retention promises were inspected by third-party security systems, which subsequently opened unique web links embedded within user prompts days later.

This matters because it reveals widespread opacity and deceptive practices in the artificial intelligence supply chain. Developers and enterprises choosing these API providers based on promises of Zero Data Retention, direct model hosting, or specific privacy standards are unknowingly having their sensitive data, images, and prompts funneled through third-party networks and processed on external cloud infrastructure subject to unexpected content moderation.

stories.author: jlelse
stories.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
stories.groq_label: AI reduces effort to configure and automate self hosted services, reigniting interest in experimenting with new infrastructure
stories.groq_explain:
The post describes how the author’s enthusiasm for self‑hosting has been revived by the practical assistance of artificial‑intelligence tools. After years of maintaining a stable but unchanging set of services, the author found that AI‑driven coding agents now make it easy to modify Docker Compose files, write scripts and adjust infrastructure with far less effort than before. Tasks that once required reading changelogs or troubleshooting for an evening can now be tried spontaneously, and many ideas that previously seemed too complex have become feasible.

AI has also lowered the barrier to experimenting with unfamiliar technologies. The author mentions finally using NixOS for a home server and creating a custom Debian‑based bootable container image, projects that would have taken a week without AI but were completed in a half‑day with its help. Learning can happen incrementally, with the AI answering questions and refining configurations on the fly.

Automation of routine DevOps work is another key benefit. By storing all configuration in Git and using tools such as Renovate to generate update pull requests, the author can merge changes from a phone and rely on GitHub or Forgejo actions to build and deploy automatically. Although these automation tools pre‑date AI, the author credits AI with finally assembling them into a cohesive workflow, resulting in far less repetitive manual work.

The renewed activity has also led to a hardware refresh. The author moved many services from a VPS back to a home server, upgrading an older ASRock DeskMini with a newer Ryzen processor and a quiet Noctua cooler, while repurposing an HP thin client as a network router. Reusing existing hardware avoids new purchases and provides the extra compute needed for further experimentation.

Finally, AI has changed the author’s approach to problems without ready‑made software. Instead of spending time searching for and adapting open‑source projects, the author now builds small custom tools—such as scripts to download invoices, e‑papers or Linux ISOs—using Go, often with AI assistance. The overall message is that AI reduces friction, accelerates learning, streamlines maintenance, and encourages both the adoption of new self‑hosting technologies and the creation of bespoke utilities.

stories.author: dverlaeckt80
stories.title: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad
stories.groq_label: Pakistani architect Kamil Khan Mumtaz is celebrated domestically for his modernist, climate‑responsive designs and conservation efforts, while remaining largely unseen abroad.
stories.groq_explain:
The article profiles Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect whose work is highly regarded in Pakistan but little known internationally. It begins with the author’s first encounter with Mumtaz’s recent buildings in Lahore, noting their confident design, high‑quality materials and detailing. The piece traces Mumtaz’s background: born in Calcutta in 1939, educated at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College, and later at the Architectural Association in London where he absorbed a modernist approach. After returning to Pakistan in 1966 he opened his practice and became involved in communist activism, which led to two imprisonments under the military regime.

Mumtaz’s early career combined modernist ideas with an interest in adapting them to local climate and materials. He produced a seminal report on the historic Walled City of Lahore, arguing for its preservation at a time when officials wanted demolition. The Walled City was eventually saved and is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the 1970s Mumtaz built workers’ housing that used local brick and arched roofs, but the design conflicted with the occupants’ preferences, prompting him to question his communication with users.

A turning point came in 1980 when Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave Mumtaz a book on Sufi tradition in Persian architecture. The text profoundly altered his perspective, leading him to abandon the purely materialist modernist stance he had held as a Marxist and atheist. Since then Mumtaz has worked to revive Pakistan’s traditional architectural language, designing homes, offices, mosques and schools that incorporate historic forms while using contemporary techniques.

The article emphasizes the challenges of finding skilled craftsmen capable of executing traditional details, noting that many such skills have dwindled worldwide. Mumtaz has collaborated with the remaining hereditary artisans, rediscovering lost practices such as specific brickwork, flat domes and muqarnas vaults. His work is praised in Pakistan for honoring cultural heritage and demonstrating that traditional forms can still be built with modern quality. The piece argues that Mumtaz’s relative obscurity abroad reflects a broader neglect by global architecture publications of the rich building culture present in Lahore and Pakistan.

stories.author: liamg
stories.title: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount
stories.groq_label: Company culture is measured by dividing custom Slack emojis by the square root of headcount
stories.groq_explain:
The article titled Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount presents a lighthearted and satirical alternative to traditional corporate methods of measuring company culture. The author argues that standard attempts to track or construct culture—such as employee surveys, values posters, corporate offsites, and bizarre interview questions—are artificial, expensive, and ineffective. Instead of relying on HR slide decks, the author suggests an objective and non-intrusive metric based on custom Slack emoji.

The central concept is the Emoji Coefficient, calculated by taking the total number of custom emoji in a Slack workspace and dividing it by the square root of the total user headcount. Using the square root accounts for emoji being a shared resource across the organization, meaning a company of ten thousand employees does not need ten thousand times more emoji than a small startup. 

The score provides a snapshot of organizational health. A coefficient under five indicates a sterile environment where employees rely strictly on default reactions and work solely for their paycheck. Scores between five and twenty reflect a functional, healthy organization, while scores between twenty and fifty describe a thriving workplace. Scores fifty and above indicate late-stage culture, where emoji become highly complex, self-referential memes that confuse management and human resources.

To prevent the metric from hiding underlying issues, the author introduces the Participation Rate, which measures the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one custom emoji. If fewer than twenty percent of employees contribute emoji, the company culture relies too heavily on a small handful of individuals and will erode when they leave. A higher participation rate ensures a broad cultural baseline. The piece also notes potential ways the metric can be gamed, such as managers uploading hundreds of company logos or mass layoffs artificially raising the score by shrinking the headcount.

This perspective matters because it highlights the futility of forced corporate initiatives. True company culture cannot be manufactured through leadership slogans or mandatory fun. Instead, it emerges organically from the bottom up, built on shared inside jokes and everyday interactions among team members.

stories.author: zerosegfaults
stories.title: Rvoip 0.5 the complete VoIP stack in Rust
stories.groq_label: rvoip is a Rust library delivering a full VoIP stack including SIP, RTP, WebRTC, and media handling in a single package without external servers
stories.groq_explain:
Rvoip 0.5 is a Rust library that provides a complete Voice over IP (VoIP) stack, allowing developers to build communication applications without needing external SIP servers, media servers, or RTP engines. The library bundles signalling, media handling, codecs, NAT traversal, security and a conversation model into a single workspace of Rust crates. The design enables a call to travel directly from application code to the network, and the same set of crates have been validated for interoperability with major telephony platforms such as Asterisk, FreeSWITCH, Jambonz, Kamailio and OpenSIPS.

The project emphasizes rapid start‑up: adding a single dependency on rvoip‑sip and tokio is sufficient to create a functional call between two endpoints on a laptop with no additional software. The documentation includes a short example where two endpoints, Alice and Bob, are created, a call is placed, answered, and then hung up, all running on the loopback interface. Larger examples progress through real microphone audio, registration to a PBX, hold and DTMF, transfers, SRTP and TLS, IVR, B2BUA, and finally browser‑based and voice‑AI gateways.

Performance measurements are provided for version 0.5.0 using an AWS c8i.4xlarge instance. In the RFC 7501/7502 benchmark, the library achieved a maximum call‑setup rate of over eight thousand calls per second for SIP over TLS and UDP signalling‑only scenarios, with sub‑millisecond median setup times. When media (G.711) is added over TLS with SRTP or UDP with RTP, the maximum call‑setup rates drop to roughly one thousand calls per second, still maintaining low latency. The tests were conducted with the library acting as a terminating endpoint that echoes media, and the results show that the system can reject excess load with fast 503 responses and recover cleanly when load decreases. Certain capabilities such as B2BUA/relay mode, registrations, transcoding, WebRTC (DTLS‑SRTP) and failover have not yet been benchmarked.

The workspace contains 47 crates, but developers only need to depend on a single crate that pulls in the necessary components. The primary product crate is rvoip‑sip, which carries a signed interoperability attestation and is intended for any telephony‑focused application. The top‑level rvoip crate re‑exports rvoip‑sip and adds an orchestrator plus optional transports and extensions that can be enabled through Cargo feature flags. Feature groups cover use cases such as a SIP phone, PBX, IVR, registrar, proxy, B2BUA, trunk gateway, SIP or WebRTC callers connected to a hosted voice agent, custom speech‑to‑text or text‑to‑speech pipelines, native mobile or embedded client SDKs, Amazon Connect integration, and media over QUIC.

For carriers evaluating the stack, the documentation points to a “For carriers” section that discusses standards coverage, performance and reliability. An upgrade path from version 0.3 is provided via a migration guide that details code changes for each breaking modification. The repository also includes example programs and deployment bundles that package the necessary crates for specific scenarios, such as SIP endpoints, carrier‑grade SIP services, browser gateways, AI conversation agents, and full pure‑Rust or native deployments. Backend integrations for authentication, directory services, storage, auditing and security protocols are available as separate rvoip‑* extension crates. Overall, rvoip 0.5 aims to deliver a fully integrated, high‑performance, pure‑Rust VoIP solution that can be embedded directly into applications without external infrastructure.

stories.author: chrhenning
stories.title: An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning
stories.groq_label: Machine learning models carry epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties that must be accounted for when making decisions.
stories.groq_explain:
This article provides an intuitive introduction to the concept and application of uncertainty in machine learning. Because machine learning relies heavily on probabilistic modeling, virtually all models contain uncertainty. Understanding and modeling this uncertainty is critical because models are inherently simplified representations of reality, and estimating confidence helps turn model outputs into effective real-world decisions.

The text divides uncertainty into two primary categories: epistemic and aleatoric. Epistemic uncertainty stems from a lack of knowledge or data about the true relationship between inputs and outputs, meaning it can be reduced by gathering more training data. Aleatoric uncertainty comes from unobserved variables or inherent variability that prevents inputs from fully dictating the outcome, so collecting more data of the same type will not eliminate it. Measuring richer inputs can sometimes transform aleatoric uncertainty into epistemic uncertainty, though fundamental limits exist when key factors cannot be measured, such as chaotic atmospheric conditions in weather forecasting.

Quantifying uncertainty matters because a single point prediction conceals plausible alternative outcomes and tail risks. The article outlines several practical benefits of modeling uncertainty:
First, predictions are distinct from decisions, and knowing the likelihood of an outcome allows humans to evaluate options based on specific risks and stakes.
Second, models can utilize selective automation to pass uncertain cases to human operators when confidence is low.
Third, active learning and Bayesian optimization use uncertainty to determine where acquiring new data will be most beneficial.
Fourth, systems like sensor fusion and Kalman filters use uncertainty estimates to weigh and combine inputs from multiple imperfect sources, such as integrating precise camera directions with accurate radar depth readings.

To illustrate these concepts, the author introduces a practical example of predicting a car's steering angle from camera images. At a road split, drivers in the middle lane might turn left half the time and right half the time. A model making a single point prediction might average these choices and suggest driving straight into a divider, which is incorrect. Instead, machine learning aims to estimate the full conditional probability distribution of outputs given the inputs, ensuring that multiple valid choices are recognized rather than compressed into a single risky estimate.

stories.author: ppmpreetham
stories.title: Largest 2D Chart library in the world using BUI: BlenderUI
stories.groq_label: BUI Charts provides 80 customizable and interactive 2D chart components for Rust applications using BlenderUI.
stories.groq_explain:
BUI Charts is a Rust-based 2D charting component library built for the BUI (BlenderUI) framework. It offers a large collection of data visualization options, consisting of 7 core base charts and 73 derived charts for a total of 80 chart types, accompanied by hundreds of runnable examples. The project provides creative control over data presentation directly inside Rust application user interfaces.

Developers can add BUI Charts to their Rust projects using Cargo by linking to the BlenderUI repository. Charts are defined as components using the rsx macro syntax and styled with utility classes. Data can be supplied directly using vectors, signals, or custom datasets. Instead of requiring users to reshape their data models to fit the library, charts extract required values via small closure functions. Charts monitor state signals and automatically redraw when data updates.

The library includes built-in interactive features, performance optimizations, and design integrations. Charts support hover tooltips with fading effects, interactive legends that toggle series visibility and rescale axes, wheel and pinch zooming on axes, and range selection by dragging. The charts automatically adapt to active application color themes, including light, dark, and custom palettes. To optimize performance, chart layout calculations are cached and only run when data, size, theme, or hidden series change, ensuring that hover events remain quick and lightweight.

stories.author: gary23w
stories.title: Show HN: Fuck_data_brokers.py
stories.groq_label: A free Python script automates legal opt out requests to delete personal data from data brokers
stories.groq_explain:
The repository hosts a single Python script called fuck_data_brokers.py that is meant to help individuals remove their personal information from data‑broker companies. The author describes their part‑time work of manually opting people out of these services and notes that the scale of data collection has exploded since the release of GPT‑4, making it impossible to handle for everyone without massive resources. To address this, the author created a free, dependency‑free tool that runs locally on a user’s computer, keeps all personal details private, and generates legal deletion and opt‑out letters for each broker.

The script first obtains a list of more than six hundred registered data‑broker companies. For each one it drafts a formal request that references the relevant privacy law for the user’s location, then either creates ready‑to‑send email messages or provides links to the brokers’ web forms. It can send the emails through the user’s own mailbox, supporting major providers such as Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and iCloud, using a one‑time app password without storing credentials. If a broker requires a web form, the tool produces a page with direct links and copy‑ready text so the user can complete the CAPTCHA and submit manually.

When a broker replies, the user can paste the response into the program and it will analyze the reply, identify the broker’s excuse, and generate a suitable follow‑up. The tool also tracks brokers that remain silent and advises where to file complaints. All interactions are performed without any external account, subscription, or artificial‑intelligence service, although the author mentions an optional “Agent Garrett” service that automates the process for a fee and a way to integrate the script with an AI assistant that supports the MCP protocol.

To use the script the user needs Python 3.8 or newer and an email address. The workflow involves running the script, entering basic personal information (name, email, city, jurisdiction), generating batches of letters, sending them, and then processing any replies. The author encourages people to star the GitHub repository, arguing that each star adds pressure on the brokers to comply with opt‑out requests.

Overall, the project provides a low‑cost, self‑hosted method for individuals to exercise their privacy rights against a large number of data‑broker firms, aiming to reduce the proliferation of personal data sold without consent. It matters because it empowers users to take concrete legal action without needing significant technical expertise or financial resources, addressing the growing concern over data exploitation in the age of advanced AI‑driven scraping.

stories.author: Bender
stories.title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' Indicted for Wire Fraud
stories.groq_label: CTO and co‑founder of RansomwareHelp was indicted for wire fraud after allegedly paying ransomware groups for decryption keys and overcharging victims.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports that Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, the chief technology officer and co‑founder of ransomwarehelp.com, has been indicted on wire‑fraud charges after an FBI sting revealed that his company was not delivering the “advanced cryptographic tools” it claimed could restore data locked by ransomware. The Florida‑based firm advertised a 99 percent success rate, a team of 80 experts and a policy of never paying ransom holders. In reality, investigators discovered that Palacio routinely paid ransomware groups for decryption keys and then billed victims far more than the amount he had paid.  

In the sting operation, FBI agents posed both as a victim organization and as a fictitious ransomware gang. After the fake victim sent a copy of a bogus ransom note, RansomwareHelp reiterated its no‑payment policy, but Palacio subsequently contacted the fake ransomware group and asked for the lowest possible price. The agents quoted .2 bitcoin, roughly $13 000. Within two days Palacio told the fake victim that the decryption would cost $13 260, and the next day he negotiated the price with the fake ransomware group down to $4 000. The indictment says the final agreed price was about $6 000 in bitcoin, yet Palacio charged the victim $16 010, including a $2 750 diagnostic fee.  

The article also cites Paul Ihme, co‑founder of security firm Soteria, who recalled a 2024 incident where an accounting firm paid a diagnostic fee to RansomwareHelp for a LockBit infection. RansomwareHelp proposed a recovery price of $438 880, claiming to use “510 preconfigured forensic servers” and extensive brute‑force decryption processes. The firm demanded unrestricted remote access via AnyDesk, which Ihme believes was used to delete ransomware notes from the victim’s network, preventing the victim from contacting the attackers directly. A screenshot of a 2024 chat shows RansomwareHelp negotiating with LockBit and urging the gang not to reveal the negotiations to the victim, which annoyed the attackers.  

The indictment matters because it exposes a fraudulent business model that preyed on organizations already victimized by ransomware, charging exorbitant fees while merely acting as a middleman that paid the attackers for decryption keys. It highlights the risks of relying on unverified third‑party recovery services and underscores the importance of law‑enforcement vigilance in exposing such scams.

stories.author: iantongeorge
stories.title: YouTube Ad Punisher – Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays
stories.groq_label: YouTube Ad Punisher automatically reloads videos when ads appear, preserving the timestamp to eliminate ads
stories.groq_explain:
YouTube Ad Punisher is a browser extension designed to eliminate YouTube advertisements by automatically reloading the page the moment an ad is detected, while preserving the viewer’s exact playback position. The tool observes the YouTube page for visual cues of an ad, such as the presence of an .ad‑showing class, skip‑ad buttons or overlay elements, checks for these every half second and also uses a MutationObserver. When an ad is found it records the current video timestamp, reloads the page with the timestamp added to the URL, and lets YouTube automatically seek back to that point, effectively resuming playback without the ad. The process repeats up to three times; if the ad persists after three reloads the extension redirects the user to an ad‑free mirror site called yout‑ube.com with looping disabled.  

In addition to skipping ads, the extension builds a local database of every ad it encounters. For each ad it stores the detection time, advertiser name, video title, playback position before the reload, ad duration and any skip‑button text. Users can view this history through a popup attached to the extension icon and can export the data as JSON or CSV. The extension requires only storage and tab permissions on YouTube domains and does not transmit any data externally.  

Installation is straightforward for Chrome‑based browsers (Chrome, Brave, Edge, Opera) by loading the unpacked repository folder, and a zip release is also available. An experimental Safari workflow uses an AppleScript helper to inject the same JavaScript into the page, though it may need occasional manual adjustments.  

The underlying concept exploits the fact that YouTube serves ads as part of the initial page load. A reload causes YouTube to reassess whether to insert an ad, and after one or two reloads the ad slot is often empty, allowing the video to play uninterrupted. Because this technique works on the client side, it avoids detection by YouTube’s anti‑ad‑block mechanisms and does not rely on network‑level blocking lists. The author notes that widespread use would increase page‑load requests while reducing ad impressions, turning each reload into a passive protest against unwanted advertising.  

YouTube Ad Punisher can be combined with traditional blockers such as uBlock Origin and segment‑skipping tools like SponsorBlock without conflict, providing a layered approach to an ad‑free viewing experience. Limitations include occasional breakage when YouTube changes its DOM class names, and the inability to preserve timestamps for certain live‑stream mid‑roll ads, which are handled by a plain reload. The project’s source includes a manifest for Chrome extension version three, content scripts for detection and reload logic, a popup UI for history viewing, and a minimal background service worker.

stories.author: julianlam
stories.title: AMD Specific Patches for Llama.cpp
stories.groq_label: llama-cpp-rdna-boosts adds AMD specific patches that raise llama.cpp token generation to 55 tokens per second and prefill to 1300 tokens per second
stories.groq_explain:
The article introduces a set of AMD‑specific patches for the llama.cpp inference engine, packaged as the repository llama‑cpp‑rdna‑boosts. The author recommends this fork for anyone with an AMD graphics card because it provides a lightweight set of changes that markedly increase both pre‑fill and token‑generation throughput. In the author’s tests the token generation speed rose from roughly thirty‑five to fifty‑five tokens per second, while pre‑fill performance more than doubled from seven hundred to thirteen hundred tokens per second.

The piece places these patches in the broader context of a recent surge of specialized inference engines that have emerged as of November 2026. Projects such as Strata, Basalt, and RustingStrata are highlighted as examples that prioritize a narrow set of models or hardware, chase ever‑higher token rates, and often rely on aggressive model‑level modifications to achieve speed. The author notes that while these engines can achieve impressive results, their optimizations sometimes involve altering how the model operates rather than focusing purely on hardware‑specific improvements.

Against this backdrop, llama‑cpp‑rdna‑boosts is presented as an alternative that stays close to the stable base of llama.cpp, applying only a minimal set of AMD‑targeted enhancements. The changes are maintained as a small patch set that is repeatedly reapplied to newer llama.cpp commits, reducing maintenance complexity. The documentation, though somewhat informal, outlines the modifications and preserves transparency.

Installation is straightforward for users with ROCm libraries: pre‑built container images are available on GitHub Container Registry. The author provides a sample podman command that pulls the server‑rocm‑10.1 image, mounts the model directory, and exposes the necessary devices and network settings. The author also mentions that updating the system would simply involve pulling a newer image, though this has not yet been tested.

Performance testing was carried out on an AMD R9700 GPU connected via an eGPU to a laptop, using the Swift‑1.5‑Qwen3.8‑27B‑GGUF model with MTP enabled. The reported figures confirm the claimed improvements in both pre‑fill and token generation. The author contrasts this experience with other AMD‑focused forks such as vllm‑radiance, noting that the latter’s build process was cumbersome and the resulting engine overengineered for a single‑machine, single‑developer workflow.

In conclusion, the article praises the rdna‑boosts community for delivering tangible speed gains while adhering to a lean, maintainable approach, and expresses enthusiasm for future developments from that project.

stories.author: rxliuli
stories.title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
stories.groq_label: SimDrop integrates running iOS simulators into the Finder sidebar for easy drag‑and‑drop file transfer.
stories.groq_explain:
SimDrop is a macOS utility that makes each booted iOS simulator appear as a folder in the Finder sidebar, allowing users to drag files into and out of the simulator’s Photos library and Files‑app Downloads directory. When a simulator starts, a folder named after the device (for example iPhone Duo) is created under the sidebar location SimDrop → Locations. Inside that folder are two subfolders: Photos and Videos, which show the simulator’s photo library, and Downloads, which maps to the simulator’s Files‑app storage.

The app is distributed as a Homebrew cask (brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop) and as a signed DMG on GitHub releases. It runs on macOS 15 or later and must be allowed to operate unsandboxed because it drives simctl and accesses the simulator’s file system directly. After installing, the user opens SimDrop once to grant two one‑time approvals: enabling the background helper in System Settings → General → Login Items, and activating the Finder extension via the banner or under File Providers. Once approved, SimDrop works silently in the background and persists across restarts.

Dragging behavior follows the standard Finder rules: moving a file within the same volume transfers it, while dragging across volumes copies it. Because the File Provider locations reside in ~/Library/CloudStorage on the startup disk, dragging a file from the Desktop into a simulator’s Downloads folder moves the file. Holding the Option key while dragging forces a copy. Moving files out of the simulator’s Downloads also moves them back to the Mac, while files dropped into the Photos or Videos folder are imported via simctl addmedia and appear in the simulator’s Photos app. Photos are displayed as thumbnails without prior download, and any non‑image/video file dropped into the Photos folder is redirected to the Downloads folder, with SimDrop posting a notification about the location.

The Downloads folder supports adding, opening, replacing, deleting and restoring files. Deleting a file sends it to the Mac’s Trash and removes it from the simulator; restoring puts it back. Deleting a photo in Finder moves it to the simulator’s “Recently Deleted” album, where it remains recoverable for 30 days. The utility refreshes the Finder view a few seconds after changes made inside the simulator.

SimDrop works only with iOS simulators; real devices are not supported because iOS does not expose the Files‑app storage over USB and does not import photos written to the device’s DCIM folder. The architecture consists of three components: the SimDrop app (which registers a launch‑at‑login helper and a File Provider domain), a launchd helper that watches the simulator device directory and invokes simctl commands, and a Finder extension that implements an NSFileProviderReplicatedExtension to read and write the simulator folders directly using a temporary‑exception entitlement. The helper signals the extension to refresh the working set after changes, and it edits the simulator’s Photos.sqlite database directly to mark deletions.

Implementation notes mention that the helper must run as a plain executable inside SimDrop.app; placing it in a separate bundle prevents the enumerator signal from working. The extension tracks a snapshot of the working set to report deletions, and it does not delete items from Finder unless they are explicitly removed from that set. Overall, SimDrop provides a convenient way for developers to manage files and media in running iOS simulators directly from the macOS Finder.

stories.author: e12e
stories.title: Nextcloud Office Desktop app
stories.groq_label: Nextcloud Office Desktop app provides a free, cross‑platform office suite with offline editing and real‑time collaboration via Nextcloud Hub.
stories.groq_explain:
Nextcloud announced the first production‑ready version of Euro‑Office on June 9 2026 as part of the Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer release. Euro‑Office is a sovereign collaborative office suite that is developed and governed in Europe, and it powers the new Nextcloud Office Desktop app. The app is free and open source and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, offering editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations and PDFs with high compatibility for Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP).

The desktop app lets users work offline, keep files locally, and switch seamlessly between the browser‑based Nextcloud Hub and the desktop client. Users can connect the app to one or more Nextcloud instances by adding the cloud URL and logging in, after which they can open, edit and co‑edit files in real time. Because the app uses the fonts installed on the local machine, users can employ corporate or custom fonts without involving Nextcloud administrators, though collaborators without the same fonts will see fallback fonts.

Digital signatures and file protection are built in. Users can sign documents, spreadsheets or presentations with a digital certificate, add passwords, and restrict actions such as commenting, form filling or editing with tracked changes only. The app also includes a Protection tab for these security options.

Installation packages are available on the official Nextcloud installation page. Windows builds are provided for x64 and ARM64, Linux packages are offered as .deb for Debian‑based distributions and .rpm for Fedora, and a macOS version is supplied for Apple Silicon. Unsigned builds and source code can be obtained from GitHub, where users are invited to report issues, submit feature ideas, contribute code, or help with translations. Contributions must remain compatible with the project’s AGPL v3 license.

The release matters because it gives Nextcloud users a fully offline‑capable, cross‑platform office suite that aligns with European data‑sovereignty goals, integrates tightly with Nextcloud’s collaborative platform, and provides enterprise‑grade features such as digital signatures and file protection without requiring separate proprietary software.

stories.author: saikatsg
stories.title: Intel One Mono font (2023)
stories.groq_label: Intel One Mono is a free open‑source monospaced developer font optimized for legibility, low‑vision accessibility, and extensive language support.
stories.groq_explain:
Intel One Mono is an open‑source monospaced typeface created for developers, especially those with low vision, to improve readability and reduce eye strain and coding errors. The design was carried out by Frere‑Jones Type in collaboration with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, and it incorporated feedback from a panel of low‑vision and legally blind programmers throughout the process. The family supports more than two hundred Latin‑script languages and is offered in four weights—Light, Regular, Medium and Bold—with matching italic styles.  

The fonts are distributed under a free open‑source license and can be downloaded from the project’s release page. Intel recommends using the OpenType (.otf) or TrueType (.ttf) formats for desktop applications, the .ttf format for mobile apps, and the .woff and .woff2 formats for web use. For optimal legibility the fonts have been manually tuned for screen display, particularly on Windows, and are best viewed at seven points or larger in print and nine pixels or larger on screen.  

Developers can activate Intel One Mono in popular code editors by setting the font family to Intel One Mono in the editor’s preferences. Programming ligatures are available through OpenType stylistic set ss01, and additional optional features include arrow‑style less‑than‑or‑equal and greater‑than‑or‑equal symbols (ss02), a “www” ligature (ss03), an alternate three (ss04), and a raised colon (ss11 or ss12). Language support is handled by the ccmp and locl features, and superscript, subscript, numerator and denominator glyphs can be accessed via standard OpenType features.  

The repository also provides the complete editable source files in UFO format. Separate subfolders contain the source instances for each style and outline files for PostScript (.otf) and TrueType (.ttf, .woff, .woff2) builds. Users can edit these sources with RoboFont or other compatible editors, then generate installable fonts by using the editor’s generate function with recommended settings such as decomposition and autohinting for .otf builds, and autohinting alone for TrueType‑based builds. More advanced users can edit the master files that define the extreme points of the design space and then interpolate to produce the full range of weights.  

Overall, Intel One Mono offers a developer‑focused, highly legible monospaced font with extensive language coverage, open licensing, and customizable OpenType features, along with full source files for those who wish to modify or extend the typeface.

stories.author: ritzaco
stories.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
stories.groq_label: Google will mandate its Model Context Protocol servers for AI agents accessing Workspace APIs, restricting key actions like sending emails.
stories.groq_explain:
This article explains that Google is changing how artificial intelligence agents interact with Google Workspace applications such as Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Docs. Effective February 1, 2027, a new clause in Google API terms requires any software tool that is an AI agent or driven by an AI model to connect to Workspace using Google official Model Context Protocol servers. Tools that do not involve artificial intelligence, such as automated backup jobs or basic database sync scripts, are exempt and can continue using standard APIs normally.

The main issue introduced by this policy is a severe restriction on functionality, particularly for Gmail. The public Gmail server allows AI tools to read threads, search mail, list labels, and create initial drafts. However, it completely lacks the capability to send, reply, forward, or edit existing drafts. Those full email features exist but are restricted to approved partners. Similarly, the Drive server lacks features like moving, renaming, or sharing files. As a result, large partners can build tools that send emails and share files, while independent developers cannot offer these actions through public servers and are forbidden from falling back to traditional APIs to achieve them.

The policy also introduces strict privacy and data rules for AI developers. Developers can only process Workspace data to complete active, user-authorized tasks and must erase the data when the user disconnects. Additionally, retained technical data like vector embeddings, user profiles, and memory indexes built from Workspace content cannot be kept for more than thirty days. Developers are strictly prohibited from using Workspace data for training models, performing evaluations, or building competing products.

This change matters significantly to software developers, businesses, and users relying on AI assistants for workplace automation. Developers building email assistants or productivity plugins must adapt to these mandatory servers within a limited timeframe, alter their workflows to accommodate restricted feature sets, or seek formal partner status with Google. For end users, independent AI tools will become far less capable than official partner integrations, fundamentally changing the landscape of custom AI automation on Google Workspace.

stories.author: seizethecheese
stories.title: OpenAI may be in cost control mode
stories.groq_label: Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 are cost‑tuned models that generate fewer output and reasoning tokens, making them underthinking outliers compared to earlier versions.
stories.groq_explain: The article examines recent releases from OpenAI—Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2—and argues that these models have been deliberately tuned for cost savings. Using proprietary data, the author shows that both the number of output tokens per task and the number of reasoning tokens per task have decreased compared with earlier versions. A chart (described but not reproduced) plots the ratio of spending of the GPT model versus competing models on the X‑axis and Elo score from a leaderboard on the Y‑axis, indicating a shift in performance and cost. A second chart compares the amount of reasoning a model performs relative to opponents, with points above the line indicating more reasoning and points below indicating less; Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 fall well below the line, making them outliers for reduced reasoning. Similar patterns are seen in output token usage. Statistical tests support the significance of these changes: the p‑value for output token reduction is 0.0055 for Sol and 0.022 for Astra, while the p‑value for reasoning reduction is 0.00013 for Sol and 0.0064 for Astra. The conclusion is that Astra and Sol have been cost‑tuned to the extent that they now under‑think compared with their predecessors, suggesting OpenAI is prioritizing lower operational costs over model depth of reasoning. This matters because it may affect the quality and capabilities of OpenAI’s newer models, potentially influencing user experience and competitive positioning in the AI market.

stories.author: joonehur
stories.title: Lions' Commentary on Unix: Why It Was Secretly Copied for 20 Years
stories.groq_label: John Lions' commentary on Unix gave generations of students essential access to Unix source code, circulating unofficially for twenty years before an official edition was released.
stories.groq_explain:
John Lions, a professor at the University of New South Wales, wrote his own textbook to teach operating systems because the Unix source code was the most effective learning material. Early in his career the Unix source could be examined in class, but in June 1979 AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms at the USENIX conference that prohibited courses from disclosing or discussing the source code. This restriction meant that Lions’ book, which contained the Unix Version 6 source and his commentary, had to be distributed under tight control. 

For roughly twenty years before an official edition was finally published, computer‑science students relied on unauthorized photocopies of Lions’ commentary. The book became a crucial resource for a generation of students who wanted to understand operating‑system internals and eventually build their own systems. The demand for the text is illustrated by a dramatized scene in which authorities try to seize copies, while a student argues that only the source code can provide true insight, not just system‑call theory. 

The article notes that a reconstructed version of the commentary is now available as a PDF and that printed copies can be ordered from Amazon. The Unix Version 6 source code itself can be obtained separately from the TUHS archive. Several references are listed, including the original Lions’ Commentary with source code, historical accounts of the licensing restrictions, and correspondence that led to the eventual publication. The piece highlights how the book’s unofficial circulation helped shape operating‑system education despite legal barriers, and it underscores the lasting impact of Lions’ work on teaching materials such as MIT’s xv6 teaching operating system.

stories.author: hn-aarvin
stories.title: NormalScript: A perfectly normal scripting language
stories.groq_label: NormalScript provides a lightweight JavaScript subset virtual machine that embeds in Node or Bun for fast script execution with pause and resume support
stories.groq_explain:
NormalScript is a lightweight virtual machine that executes a subset of JavaScript inside a Node or Bun application. It is offered as a pure JavaScript package for Node version 24 or later and Bun version 1.4 or later, requiring no WebAssembly modules, native add‑ons, or separate worker processes. By providing a small set of host functions, developers can embed NormalScript as a library and run short scripts, plugins, or agent code directly within their existing process.

The core capabilities include embedded scripting without a second runtime, fast start‑up because there is no worker to spawn, and the ability to pause a running script, serialize its state to bytes, and later resume it on any process that uses the same build and host definitions. Scripts are compiled to bytecode and run on a compact virtual machine, with execution terminating on a configurable timeout or an abort signal.

NormalScript supports a modern, strict‑mode subset of JavaScript that includes async functions, generators, classes, top‑level await, and return statements. The host API is promise‑based and provides utilities such as Host.fn to expose ordinary functions as globals, Host.namespace for lazy catalogs, Host.durableFn for long‑running operations, and StreamingResponse for streaming bodies. Errors are returned with a kind, a message, and optional suggestions.

Runtime creation is performed with Runtime.make, which takes a function that supplies globals and optional limits such as maximum execution time and output size. Each run receives its own globals, and host calls may be synchronous or asynchronous, with results copied back to the script using JSON‑like serialization. The system defines caps for strings, arrays, pending promises, and nesting depth, and exceeding these limits throws a RangeError inside the script.

A notable feature is the suspend‑save‑resume workflow. A running program can be paused with program.suspend, its state converted to bytes with toBytes, stored, and later reconstructed with fromBytes and runtime.resume. Snapshots are tied to the specific build that created them; mismatched builds or malformed data cause a SnapshotError. Idempotent host calls are rerun on resume, while non‑idempotent calls are not repeated.

Operational details include how runs start, stop, and pause, how host calls are handled concurrently, and how cancellation propagates via AbortSignal. Limits on active time, output bytes, and resource caps are documented, and there is no separate step‑count or memory limit beyond those fixed caps.

NormalScript is marketed as a “perfectly normal” scripting language trusted by over four hundred organizations, licensed under MIT, and positioned for teams that need lightweight, embedded scripting capabilities without the overhead of a separate JavaScript engine. Its ability to pause and resume scripts, combined with a minimal runtime footprint, makes it suitable for plugins, workflows, and agent‑style code that must run inside existing Node or Bun services.

stories.author: Herrera
stories.title: OpenAI cuts GPT-6.2 usage: Astra hits limits 40% faster, Sol 25% faster

stories.author: rguiscard
stories.title: Minipg: PostgreSQL as a Single Executable
stories.groq_label: Minipg packages PostgreSQL into a single executable that runs databases from a .pgdb directory without separate server setup
stories.groq_explain:
Minipg is a tool that packages PostgreSQL into a single executable, eliminating the need for a separately configured server. A directory with the .pgdb extension holds all of the database’s data, configuration files, credentials, and the specific PostgreSQL version. Running the command minipg followed by the .pgdb path opens a psql shell, creating the directory if it does not already exist. The executable starts a PostgreSQL server only when a command requires it and shuts the server down automatically when it becomes idle.

The project embeds the official Docker Hub postgres:18‑alpine image and runs it using the h9 library, which provides a Plan 9 kernel that handles system calls for the Alpine PostgreSQL binaries. This approach avoids the need for a full Linux kernel, virtual‑machine image, or Docker installation on the host. In continuous‑integration environments the Linux binary is static, requires no special privileges, and can run without /dev/kvm by using h9’s native backend.

A web‑based demo is available; it downloads about 35 MB and runs inside the browser using JavaScript Promise integration, v86 (an x86 emulator), and xterm.js for the terminal interface. The demo runs the Linux build of minipg inside the PostgreSQL image itself, starts PostgreSQL as ordinary processes, and serves connections over a Unix socket because a web page cannot use TCP.

Typical usage examples include launching a psql shell, executing a single SQL statement, retrieving the connection URL, running a foreground server, starting an application with the DATABASE_URL environment variable set, and dumping or restoring a database. The .pgdb directory contains a minipg.toml file with settings and a generated superuser password, as well as a pgdata subdirectory that stores PostgreSQL’s data files in plain format. Because the data directory is just a normal folder, a stopped database can be copied like any other directory. New clusters are created from a template built at compile time, using PostgreSQL’s built‑in C.UTF‑8 locale to ensure consistent sorting across platforms.

Internally, exactly one PostgreSQL process is allowed per .pgdb, enforced by a lock. The server runs inside an h9 machine whose root filesystem is the unpacked Docker image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image’s docker‑entrypoint.sh script initializes the cluster on first start. Commands such as psql or pg_dump launch short‑lived h9 machines (about ninety milliseconds to start) that share the same root. Supported host platforms include Linux on x86_64 with KVM, Linux on arm64 with KVM, and macOS on Apple Silicon using the Hypervisor.framework.

The source code is hosted on GitHub under the MIT license. Building the project requires Zig 0.16, plus standard utilities such as curl, jq, tar, and xz. The repository includes make targets to build the executable, fetch the appropriate root image for the host architecture, and generate the web demo.

A warning notes that minipg is still early‑stage and that h9’s Linux personality is immature. On h9’s native backend PostgreSQL runs roughly twice as slow as native for a single client and performs worse under load, so the tool should not be trusted with data that cannot be regenerated. Users are encouraged to report bugs and ask questions via GitHub issues.

Related projects include h9 (which runs native 9front executables and Linux binaries on host hypervisors), the official PostgreSQL Docker image, the v86 x86 emulator used for the demo, and xterm.js, the terminal component of the web interface.

stories.author: miohtama
stories.title: Bare Metal Qwen
stories.groq_label: A 24 KB pure‑assembly OS boots Qwen3‑0.6B LLM directly on x86‑64 hardware or KVM.
stories.groq_explain:
Bare‑Metal Qwen is a project that provides a self‑contained, bootable x86‑64 operating system written entirely in assembly. The OS loads the Qwen 3‑0.6B language model directly from RAM and runs it without any underlying Linux, Windows, C, Rust, or libc runtime. The kernel is a stripped static Multiboot 1 binary of about 24 KB, which can be built in two variants: a fast Q8 mode that uses 8‑bit quantisation (default) and a legacy FP32 mode. Once loaded, the system can decode tokens at roughly 135 tokens per second on a 16‑core AMD EPYC EPYC 7642 under QEMU KVM, and about 55 tokens per second on a diskless Proxmox VM using an Intel Xeon E5‑2670 v3.

The repository supplies scripts and Makefile targets for building the kernel, creating a hybrid BIOS/UEFI bootable ISO, and running the system under QEMU. Prerequisites include an x86‑64 CPU with AVX2, FMA and F16C support, and the usual development packages such as nasm, binutils and qemu. The model file is an exported .asmbin binary of either the FP16‑scaled v2 (≈ 614 MiB) or the FP32‑scaled v1 (≈ 649 MiB) format, which is memory‑mapped as zero‑copy on 2 MiB huge pages.

Three deployment options are described. Option A boots the kernel directly in QEMU using the COM1 serial console, with optional command‑line prompts for one‑shot inference or an interactive VGA console with PS/2 keyboard. Option B builds a ~661 MiB ISO that packages the kernel, GRUB2 Multiboot configuration and the model, allowing boot via legacy BIOS (SeaBIOS) or UEFI (OVMF). Option C shows how to upload the ISO to a Proxmox VE node and create a diskless VM that runs entirely from RAM; the VM must expose AVX2 and reserve at least 2 GiB of contiguous RAM for the model and KV‑cache.

When the system boots, it presents an interactive console (asm‑llm>) that operates in a multi‑turn chat mode with a persistent key‑value cache. Users can type messages, invoke built‑in commands such as /clear, /new, /reset, /think, /bench, /halt, /quit and /help, and view live context usage. The kernel accepts several command‑line parameters, for example a prompt string to run immediately after boot, maximum token limits, context length, thread count, and flags to enable or disable reasoning mode. The console works over both VGA/PS2 keyboard and serial ports simultaneously, and when the KV‑cache reaches its capacity it automatically resets. Overall, the project demonstrates that a large language model can be run on bare metal with minimal overhead, providing a fast, low‑level environment for inference without any traditional operating system.

stories.author: nb-t
stories.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
stories.groq_label: Lean 4 proof verifies the Riemann Hypothesis and Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L‑functions using only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.
stories.groq_explain:
The repository contains a Lean 4 formalization of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for Dirichlet L‑functions. It is presented as a research artifact that is not maintained and does not accept contributions. The proof is a Lean 4 translation of a proof originally due to Levent Alpöge, with assistance from Claude, an Anthropic language model. The development builds on Mathlib and relies only on the axioms propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.

Two versions of the formalization are provided. The “grh” directory holds a readable edition of roughly three hundred thousand lines of Lean code, while the “grh‑compact” directory contains a more condensed version of about seventy‑six thousand lines that proves the same five theorems. Each directory is a separate Lake project with its own README file. Instructions for building the project require Lean 4.35.0 and a specific Mathlib commit (56a00585). Building the code typically takes one to two hours on a twelve‑core machine with twenty‑four gigabytes of RAM; the time increases if the Mathlib cache is missing. After building, one can run a script to list the axioms used.

The proof has only been verified by automated machine checks; it has not been read in detail by any mathematician, and no accompanying research paper is provided. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license, with copyright belonging to Anthropic, PBC. The repository includes license files, a NOTICE document, and an ATTRIBUTION file.
